name: Amelia Brown
chief_complaint: Worsening shortness of breath and cough for 2 days
opening_statement: Amelia is a 7-year-old girl brought in by her mother with increased shortness of breath, persistent cough, and difficulty breathing that started 2 days ago after exposure to cold air at her school sports day.
emotional_baseline: Anxious and slightly scared due to breathing difficulty; cooperative but speaks in short sentences due to dyspnea; mother appears worried

symptoms.name: Dyspnea
symptoms.character: Progressive shortness of breath worse with activity
symptoms.timing: Worse at night and early morning

rag_citation.quote: Dyspnea, wheeze, and cough are cardinal symptoms of acute asthma exacerbation in children

symptoms.name: Wheeze
symptoms.character: High-pitched expiratory wheeze audible without stethoscope

rag_citation.quote: Audible wheeze indicates significant airway obstruction and moderate to severe exacerbation

symptoms.name: Cough
symptoms.timing: Worse at night (wakes from sleep 2-3 times)

rag_citation.quote: Nocturnal cough is a common presenting feature of acute asthma in children and indicates poor asthma control
Chest tightness reflects bronchospasm and is a subjective indicator of airway obstruction severity

past_medical_history.complications: 2 previous ED presentations (ages 5 and 6) for acute exacerbations

medications.name: Salbutamol (Ventolin) 100 mcg inhaler
medications.compliance: Used 8-10 times in past 24 hours (increased frequency)

allergies: No known drug allergies; environmental allergies to house dust mite and grass pollen (triggers asthma and rhinitis)
family_history: Mother has asthma (well-controlled); father has allergic rhinitis; maternal grandmother has COPD (ex-smoker); no family history of atopy in siblings (one younger brother, age 4, healthy)

social_history.living_situation: Lives with both parents and younger brother in suburban house; pet-free household (parents aware of asthma triggers)
social_history.school: Year 2 primary school student; usually attends regularly; missed 2 days of school this week due to illness
social_history.activities: Enjoys soccer and swimming (usually participates without difficulty when asthma well-controlled); recent school sports day with cold weather exposure triggered symptoms
social_history.environmental_exposures: No smokers in household; house has carpet in bedrooms (dust mite exposure); sleeps with windows closed
social_history.immunizations: Up to date per National Immunisation Program; influenza vaccine received annually

examination_findings.general_appearance: Alert, anxious child sitting upright; speaks in short sentences (3-4 words); no cyanosis; mild intercostal recession

respiratory.inspection: Tachypnea (RR 32), using accessory muscles, mild intercostal and subcostal recession
respiratory.palpation: Chest expansion symmetrical but reduced; no crepitus
respiratory.auscultation: Bilateral expiratory wheeze throughout both lung fields; prolonged expiratory phase; good air entry bilaterally; no crackles

examination_findings.cardiovascular: Tachycardia (HR 118); heart sounds dual, no murmurs; capillary refill <2 seconds; peripheral pulses present
examination_findings.abdomen: Soft, non-tender; no organomegaly; bowel sounds present
examination_findings.skin: Dry skin patches on flexor surfaces consistent with eczema (well-controlled); no rash or urticaria
examination_findings.ent: No stridor; oropharynx not inflamed; no nasal polyps on anterior rhinoscopy

bedside.interpretation: Moderate airflow obstruction indicating moderate exacerbation
Mild hypoxemia; meets criteria for oxygen therapy

laboratory.test: Not routinely required for uncomplicated asthma exacerbation
laboratory.interpretation: Blood tests indicated only if suspected infection or complications

imaging.indication: Only if suspected pneumonia, pneumothorax, or no response to treatment
imaging.expected_findings: Hyperinflation, flattened hemidiaphragms; no focal consolidation or pneumothorax in uncomplicated case

expected_management.action: Administer high-flow oxygen via Hudson mask to maintain SpO2 ≥94%
Salbutamol 6 puffs (600 mcg) via spacer, repeat every 20 minutes for first hour (or continuous nebulization 5 mg/hour if severe)
expected_management.rationale: Bronchodilator therapy is first-line for acute exacerbation; high-dose via spacer equivalent to nebulizer in moderate cases

expected_management.action: Ipratropium bromide 8 puffs (160 mcg) via spacer with salbutamol
expected_management.rationale: Combination therapy improves outcomes in moderate-severe exacerbations (eTG recommendation)

expected_management.action: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg (20 mg) stat dose, then 1 mg/kg daily for 3-5 days
expected_management.rationale: Corticosteroids reduce relapse rates and speed recovery in moderate-severe exacerbations
expected_management.mbs_item: Medication cost (PBS unrestricted for acute asthma)

expected_management.action: Reassess after 1 hour: respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, PEF, clinical signs (wheeze, recession, ability to speak)
expected_management.rationale: Determine response to treatment and need for escalation

expected_management.action: Discharge home if SpO2 >94%, PEF >75% personal best, minimal wheeze, no respiratory distress after 1-2 hours observation
expected_management.rationale: Safe discharge criteria met; continue oral corticosteroids and increase preventer therapy

expected_management.action: Admit to hospital if persistent SpO2 <94%, PEF <60%, ongoing respiratory distress, or poor response after 1 hour
expected_management.rationale: Criteria for hospital admission: severe or life-threatening features, inadequate response to initial treatment

expected_management.action: Provide written asthma action plan; increase fluticasone to 250 mcg BD for 7-14 days; review trigger avoidance (cold air, exercise technique); book GP follow-up in 2-7 days
expected_management.rationale: Post-exacerbation care reduces relapse risk; step-up preventer therapy after exacerbation per eTG guidelines

critical_errors.error: Failing to administer supplemental oxygen when SpO2 <95%
critical_errors.consequence: Hypoxemia can lead to end-organ damage; failure to correct is auto-fail
critical_errors.prevention: Always measure SpO2 in respiratory presentations; target SpO2 ≥94% in children with asthma

critical_errors.error: Not administering systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisolone) in moderate-severe exacerbation
critical_errors.consequence: Increased risk of treatment failure, relapse, and hospital admission; failure to give corticosteroids is auto-fail
critical_errors.prevention: eTG mandates corticosteroids for all but mild exacerbations; dose 1 mg/kg prednisolone for 3-5 days

critical_errors.error: Discharging patient without written asthma action plan or follow-up arrangement
critical_errors.consequence: High relapse risk; patient/parent unprepared for deterioration at home
critical_errors.prevention: Always provide action plan with PEF zones (green/yellow/red); book GP review within 2-7 days

critical_errors.error: Using adrenaline instead of salbutamol as first-line bronchodilator
critical_errors.consequence: Adrenaline is for anaphylaxis, not asthma; inappropriate drug choice is auto-fail
critical_errors.prevention: Salbutamol (beta-2 agonist) is first-line for asthma; ipratropium added in moderate-severe cases

critical_errors.error: Administering antibiotics without evidence of bacterial infection
critical_errors.consequence: Unnecessary antibiotic use; most exacerbations are viral or triggered by allergens/cold air
critical_errors.prevention: Antibiotics only if fever + purulent sputum + elevated WCC/CRP suggesting bacterial infection

critical_errors.error: Sending child home on reliever therapy alone without stepping up preventer (ICS) dose
critical_errors.consequence: High risk of recurrent exacerbation; failure to optimize controller therapy
critical_errors.prevention: eTG recommends doubling ICS dose for 7-14 days post-exacerbation; reassess asthma control at follow-up

fracp_reviews.credentials: FRACP (Paediatrics & Child Health), Staff Specialist, Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne
fracp_reviews.comments: Clinically accurate persona representing typical moderate asthma exacerbation in school-age child. Management aligns with eTG and Australian asthma guidelines (National Asthma Council). Appropriate emphasis on oxygen therapy, combined bronchodilator approach (salbutamol + ipratropium), and corticosteroids. Critical errors correctly identify life-threatening omissions (no oxygen, no steroids). Suggested addition: include mention of spacer technique assessment as common pitfall (poor technique reduces drug delivery). Otherwise excellent case for AMC clinical exam preparation.
learning_points_highlighted: High-dose salbutamol via spacer equivalent to nebulizer in moderate cases
Systemic corticosteroids mandatory in moderate-severe exacerbations
Written asthma action plan essential at discharge

fracp_reviews.credentials: FRACP (Paediatric Respiratory Medicine), Director of Paediatric Respiratory Unit, Sydney Children's Hospital
fracp_reviews.comments: Comprehensive and educationally valuable persona. Difficulty calibration appropriate for 'Medium' level: single organ system, time-critical presentation, but not life-threatening (PEF 60%, SpO2 94%). RAG citations correctly reference eTG rather than international guidelines. Social history appropriately includes trigger identification (cold air at sports day) and environmental factors (dust mite exposure). One enhancement: could mention assessment of inhaler technique at follow-up visit (common contributor to poor control). Critical errors well-chosen and reflect real-world mistakes in AMC clinical exams. Strong case for teaching acute asthma management principles.
learning_points_highlighted: PEF 60% of personal best = moderate exacerbation
Ipratropium bromide added in moderate-severe cases
Step-up ICS dose post-exacerbation for 7-14 days
Trigger avoidance counseling (cold air, exercise-induced bronchoconstriction)

learning_objectives: Recognize clinical features of moderate asthma exacerbation in children: tachypnea (RR >30), SpO2 92-95%, PEF 50-75% personal best, speaking in short sentences
Apply eTG-guided management: oxygen (SpO2 target ≥94%), high-dose salbutamol + ipratropium via spacer, systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 1 mg/kg)
Understand role of peak expiratory flow (PEF) in severity assessment: <50% = severe, 50-75% = moderate, >75% = mild

Differentiate asthma from other causes of pediatric wheeze: bronchiolitis (age <2 years, viral prodrome), foreign body aspiration (sudden onset, unilateral wheeze), anaphylaxis (urticaria, angioedema, rapid deterioration)
Implement post-exacerbation care: written asthma action plan, step-up ICS therapy for 7-14 days, GP follow-up within 2-7 days, trigger avoidance counseling
Identify critical errors that constitute AMC exam failure: no oxygen therapy, no corticosteroids, inappropriate drug choice (adrenaline for asthma), discharge without action plan
Recognize atopic triad (asthma, eczema, allergic rhinitis) and family history as risk factors for asthma exacerbations
Apply Australian-specific prescribing: PBS unrestricted prednisolone for acute asthma, authority required for high-dose ICS, MBS item 11630/11640 for GP asthma review
